headline: 28.9M parameter LLM runs on $8 ESP32-S3 microcontroller at 9 tokens/sec
summary: This breakthrough uses Google's Per-Layer Embeddings to store most of the model in flash memory, allowing a 100x larger model than previously possible on such a tiny chip.
details: A 28.9 million parameter language model now runs entirely on an $8 ESP32-S3 microcontroller, generating text at approximately 9 tokens per second. This marks a significant leap, as previous models on similar chips were limited to around 260 thousand parameters.

The key to fitting such a large model on a chip with only 512KB of SRAM is an innovative memory management technique. Instead of requiring the entire model to reside in fast memory, most of its parameters are stored in slower flash memory.

Language models largely consist of an embedding table, which is read from rather than computed on. By placing this 25 million row table in flash, only the small, active part of the model that performs computations needs to be in fast memory, dramatically reducing the fast memory footprint.

This approach leverages Google's Per-Layer Embeddings concept, originally from their Gemma 3n and Gemma 4 models. This is reportedly the first time this technique has been successfully applied to a microcontroller as small as the ESP32-S3.

The model was trained on the TinyStories dataset, enabling it to generate short, coherent narratives. While it excels in story generation, it cannot answer questions, follow complex instructions, or write code, as its reasoning component remains small.

The project's firmware, wiring instructions, and flashing steps are publicly available, alongside the training, ablation, and quantization code. Detailed results and on-chip measurements are also documented for transparency.

The work builds upon the TinyStories dataset for coherent text generation and Google's Per-Layer Embeddings for efficient model fitting. It also acknowledges the influence of Andrej Karpathy's llama2.c, which inspired many to explore tiny language models in C.
